Online Network Design with Maximum Delay
and Stochastic Arrivals

Tianhang Lu Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Ocean University of China,
Qingdao 266100, Shandong, China,
lutianhang@stu.ouc.edu.cn
Abstract

We study online network services that combine pending requests into batches. Each batch pays for its spatial service and for the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is the sum of these costs over all batches. Thus requests can share both a spatial purchase and one maximum-delay charge. We assume independent Poisson arrivals of known rates, while actual requests are revealed only upon arrival.

For stateless services, suppose that each type has an attainable minimum cost when served alone, that every batch costs at least the stand-alone minimum of each type it contains, and that one finite-cost action can serve any batch, regardless of its request multiplicities. We give a deterministic algorithm with long-run ratio of expectations e/(e−1)e/(e-1) against an unrestricted offline optimum. This factor is optimal, even allowing randomization, already at one request location. The key comparison measures the union of time intervals associated with requests. The theorem applies directly to multi-root and pair aggregation on trees. We also study facility location, where each request pays its own connection distance and the bounded-action assumption can fail. A deterministic policy gives a ratio 33 for arbitrary nonnegative opening costs. It immediately serves a finite initial set of requests, computes an assignment from their observed arrival gaps, and then keeps that assignment fixed. Its analysis combines Poisson insertion with a time-slice packing bound on the offline optimum. Every guarantee includes the full cost of completing finite inputs without an end-of-input signal.

1 Introduction

Consider a network operator collecting requests for a shared service. Opening a connection or activating a depot has a fixed cost, so the operator would like several requests to use the same service. Yet a batch cannot be postponed indefinitely: its oldest request has already been waiting, and determines how late the batch is. A younger request can join this batch without increasing its maximum waiting time. This gives two reasons to combine requests: they share both spatial resources and a single delay charge.

We study this tradeoff when each service pays its spatial cost plus the maximum waiting time of its requests. The objective is the sum of these costs over all services. This is a per-batch maximum: it is neither a deadline constraint nor the maximum wait over the entire execution. For example, requests can be aggregated to one of several roots in a tree, or pairs of endpoints can share connecting edges. A facility can also serve a batch, paying an opening cost and a separate connection distance for each request. In each case the algorithm must decide both when to act and how to serve the batch.

The corresponding additive-delay problems, in which every request pays its own wait, have been studied extensively over the last decade [6, 8, 3, 9, 4, 5, 2, 16, 15, 7, 10, 18, 17, 19, 1]. The frameworks of Azar and Touitou [4, 5] show that several spatial problems can be understood through a common temporal method. Maximum delay changes that temporal method. Splitting a batch preserves its sum of individual waiting times, but can repeat its maximum-wait charge. Conversely, adding more requests to a batch need not increase that charge at all.

Recent work already gives constant worst-case guarantees for maximum delay. Lu et al. [11] obtain the optimal deterministic factor 22 and randomized factor e/(e−1)e/(e-1) for rooted aggregation and extend their results to submodular service costs. They also give constant guarantees for mobile service with per-batch maximum delay [12]. Thus our motivation is not the absence of constant algorithms throughout the maximum-delay setting. Instead, we ask what statistical information reveals about the cost of batching, and whether that information permits a sharp guarantee under weaker assumptions on the spatial service.

In a repeated service system, historical demand may indicate how often each type of request occurs. We model this information by independent Poisson streams of known rates. A rate does not reveal an arrival time, but the probability of seeing no request during a given interval is known. This simple information turns out to be particularly useful for maximum delay. It suggests the following question.

Can arrival rates identify the unavoidable long-run cost of shared service, and can a simple causal schedule attain a sharp constant factor against an optimum that knows all realized arrivals?

For additive delay, Mari, Pawłowski, Ren, and Sankowski reported constant expectation ratios for stochastic matching [13] and rooted aggregation [14]. Their work shows how rates can guide a choice between immediate and periodic service. Maximum delay calls for a different comparison with the optimum: many waiting requests in one batch supply only one delay payment. We show that the appropriate lower-bound object is the measure of a union of time intervals. This observation leads to a sharp theorem for stateless shared services and, with a separate spatial argument, a constant guarantee for facility location.

1.1 Our contributions

We compare expected online and offline costs over increasingly long horizons on a fixed finite instance. Algorithms know the rates, observe requests as they arrive, and complete every finite input without being told when arrivals stop. The offline optimum may choose its batches and spatial services after seeing the entire input.

  • •

    An optimal guarantee for shared services. We give a deterministic algorithm with ratio e/(e−1)≈1.582e/(e-1)\approx 1.582 for a broad class of stateless services. Each type must have an attainable minimum singleton cost that lower-bounds any batch serving it. There must also be one finite-cost action that can serve all pending requests, regardless of how many have accumulated. No tree structure or submodularity assumption is required.

    The factor is optimal over this class, even for randomized algorithms: one request location already gives a matching lower bound. Our policy also gives a finite maximum wait on each fixed instance. The result shows exactly how far known arrival rates can close the gap between online and offline decisions in this class.

  • •

    Consequences for tree aggregation. Multi-root and pair aggregation on trees both satisfy these conditions and inherit the factor e/(e−1)e/(e-1). The offline optimum remains free to choose a different root for each batch in multi-root aggregation. These are applications of the shared-service theorem, rather than separate temporal algorithms.

  • •

    Facility location with individual connections. For arbitrary finite metrics and nonuniform opening costs, we obtain a deterministic algorithm with ratio 33. It immediately serves the first mm requests, where mm is the number of positive-rate types, and uses their observed arrival gaps to compute an assignment that remains fixed thereafter. No internal randomness is used. The offline optimum may send different requests at the same location to different facilities. This result requires a separate comparison: connection costs grow with the number of requests, so a universal spatial action of bounded cost need not exist.

These are long-run guarantees. The shared-service policy has a fixed maximum wait depending on the instance. The facility policy attaining the stated factor uses increasing service intervals; fixed finite intervals give factor 3​(1+ε)3(1+\varepsilon) for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 (Corollary 8.7). The finite horizon corrections are established in the proofs. We do not claim a uniform multiplicative bound for every short horizon.

For path-union costs, the same numerical factor also occurs in the adversarial randomized result of Lu et al. [11]. Here it is attained deterministically using arrival rates. The broader theorem requires only its stated singleton and universal-action conditions; in particular, the multi-root application does not rely on a claim that minimizing over roots preserves submodularity.

1.2 Our techniques

Measure shared delay by a union of time intervals.

Each request draws an interval starting at its arrival, with length equal to its cheapest individual service cost. All intervals belonging to one offline batch fit inside an interval whose length is paid by that batch’s spatial cost and maximum wait. Taking the union of request intervals therefore gives a lower bound on every offline schedule. Unlike adding their lengths, taking a union does not charge a batch’s shared delay repeatedly. Poisson rates let us compute how much of the time line is covered in expectation.

Use rates to choose between immediate and shared service.

For light demand, serving requests individually is inexpensive. For heavy demand, a long enough collection period spreads the cost of a universal service over time. Adding requests to a batch does not add individual waiting charges, which makes this second option effective. Comparing these two choices with the coverage lower bound gives the factor e/(e−1)e/(e-1). A one-location example shows why no online policy can improve the universal factor.

Handle individual connection costs separately.

For facility location, batching cannot remove the distance charged to each request. We immediately serve a finite initial set of requests and scale their observed arrival gaps to obtain independent exponential variables with the required rates. These values determine balls whose sets of contained facilities are greedily packed. Poisson insertion bounds the expected assignment cost by three times an auxiliary packing count. We apply the same packing rule at each time slice to shrinking balls associated with actual requests. Within one offline batch, at most one accepted ball contains its facility at any time. The opening and maximum wait pay for these portions; connections pay for the remaining portions. Stationarity and offline subadditivity turn this certificate into the lower bound needed to justify the assignment. The future arrival stream is independent of the initialization history, so the same comparison applies to the subsequent service phase. Initialization adds only an instance-dependent constant to expected cost.

1.3 Related work

Additive aggregation and network design.

Bienkowski et al. [6] initiated the study of aggregation on trees of arbitrary fixed depth with general delay. The deadline bounds were improved to O⁡(D)O(D) by Buchbinder et al. [8] and to DD by McMahan [15]. For general delay, Azar and Touitou [4] obtained O⁡(D2)O(D^{2}); the recent preprint of Ahmadian et al. [1] gives 2​D2D. Carrasco et al. [9] study a general set aggregation model with logarithmic dependence on the number of requests. Azar and Touitou’s later framework [5] reduces network design with deadlines or delay to offline optimization problems with an additional logarithmic loss. Set cover with delay admits polylogarithmic guarantees even without knowing future delay functions [2], and nearly matching lower bounds are known for set cover and several network design extensions [16]. These objectives sum requests’ delays; the maximum-delay accounting used here is different.

Facility location and online service.

The adversarial facility-location results of Azar and Touitou [4, 5] are complemented by the linear-delay algorithms of Bienkowski et al. [7]. The latter distinguish a one-sided model with an O⁡(log⁡m/log⁡log​m)O(\log m/\log\log m) guarantee from a two-sided model with a constant guarantee. Neither objective is the per-batch maximum used here. Azar et al. [3] introduced mobile service with delay. The general-metric guarantee became randomized O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) in [4] and deterministic O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) in [18]. A persistent mobile server has state-dependent spatial costs and lies outside our stateless theorem.

Clairvoyance and stochastic information.

Le, Umboh, and Xie [10] distinguish knowing future delay functions from observing only their current values. Touitou develops nonclairvoyant network design frameworks [17] and a nearly optimal nonclairvoyant service algorithm [19]. Our delay rule is known; the uncertainty concerns future arrivals. Mari et al. [13, 14] study known Poisson rates and report constant expectation ratios for additive-delay matching and rooted aggregation. We adopt this stochastic perspective, while replacing individual-wait accounting by interval coverage. Rates are assumed known and are not estimated by the algorithms in this paper.

Maximum delay.

Lu et al. [11] give an exact polynomial-time offline algorithm and tight deterministic and randomized online factors for rooted aggregation, extending these statements to submodular service costs. Their mobile-service work [12] gives deterministic factors 1010 on lines, 1212 on trees, and 2020 on arbitrary finite metrics. These recent preprints demonstrate that maximum delay can admit constants already under adversarial arrivals. We study how stationary arrival information yields a sharp deterministic factor for a broader stateless class and a deterministic facility policy whose assignment is fixed after initialization. Our guarantees are asymptotic expectation ratios, not improvements to those worst-case competitive bounds. In particular, the calendar’s instance-dependent completion term cannot be removed to obtain a uniform bound at every finite horizon.

1.4 Organization

Section 2 defines the model and basic Poisson facts. Section 3 develops the shared-service idea from one location through its tree applications. Section 4 explains the separate facility argument. These sections give the main results and the comparisons behind their constants. Section 5 begins the technical development. Sections 6 and 7 give the complete shared-service proof and tree verifications; Section 8 proves the facility guarantee.

2 Model and basic Poisson facts

2.1 Requests and maximum-delay batches

There are finitely many request types. Each occurrence ii has a type xix_{i}, an arrival time aia_{i}, and a service time ti≥ait_{i}\geq a_{i}. A service chooses a nonempty batch BB of pending requests and a feasible spatial action. If its spatial cost is C⁡(B)C(B) and it occurs at time tt, the total batch cost is

C⁡(B)+maxi∈B⁡(t−ai)=C⁡(B)+t−mini∈B⁡ai.C(B)+\max_{i\in B}(t-a_{i})=C(B)+t-\min_{i\in B}a_{i}.

The objective sums these costs over services. Maximum delay means one charge for the oldest request in each batch. It is neither a single maximum over the whole execution nor a deadline constraint. Simultaneous services pay their own maximum delays separately.

Services are instantaneous and have no capacity restriction. They are stateless: buying a network or opening a facility serves the current batch, without retaining a purchased network or an open facility for the next batch. The general shared-service theorem will specify two conditions on the available spatial actions. It does not cover a persistent mobile server.

For tree aggregation, a service buys the edges connecting its requests to a chosen root, or connecting the endpoints of pair requests. For facility location in a finite metric, service at ff pays an opening cost cf≥0c_{f}\geq 0 and the distance d⁡(xi,f)d(x_{i},f) for each occurrence ii. A later service pays for its spatial action again. The precise feasibility conditions are stated when each model is considered.

2.2 Poisson arrivals and the comparison

Type xx follows an independent homogeneous Poisson process of known rate λx≥0\lambda_{x}\geq 0. Its positive-rate interarrival times are independent exponentials of mean 1/λx1/\lambda_{x}. The algorithm knows the rates and spatial instance, but sees only arrivals that have already occurred. Zero-rate types can be ignored. Arrivals at a service time are observed first, and simultaneous actions are processed in execution order.

Let ITI_{T} be the arrivals in [0,T][0,T]. The algorithm receives no signal that the input has ended and must eventually serve every request. Its cost ALGT=ALG⁡(IT)\operatorname{ALG}_{T}=\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T}) includes all purchases and waiting after TT needed for completion. The offline optimum OPTT\operatorname{OPT}_{T} knows the entire realized input and is not restricted to the algorithm’s assignments or calendar. For each fixed instance with positive optimal asymptotic cost, our criterion is

RoE⁡(ALG)=lim supT→∞𝔼⁡[ALGT]𝔼⁡[OPTT].\operatorname{RoE}(\operatorname{ALG})=\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}_{T}]}{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]}. (1)

Expectations include independent algorithmic randomness when relevant. This is a ratio of expected total costs, rather than an expectation of samplewise ratios. The notation OI​(1)O_{I}(1) allows dependence on the fixed instance, but not on TT. An asymptotic guarantee does not remove the need to pay for completing the last batch.

2.3 The probability facts behind the coverage argument

A fixed interval of length ss contains λ​s\lambda s arrivals in expectation and is empty with probability e−λ​se^{-\lambda s}. Counts in disjoint intervals are independent, as are counts from different type streams. Combining independent streams adds their rates.

These facts let us compute the probability that a fixed point on the time line is covered by a request interval. If type xx covers that point whenever it arrives in a prescribed interval of length sxs_{x}, the probability that no type covers it is

∏xe−λx​sx=e−∑xλxsx.\prod_{x}e^{-\lambda_{x}s_{x}}=e^{-\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}s_{x}}.

The intervals here are fixed independently of the arrivals. We never assume the same calculation holds for a batch chosen by the offline optimum after observing the input. The more general counting identities used in the facility and sharpness proofs are developed in Section 5.

3 Shared service: from one location to a general theorem

We begin with one request location. This example explains both the algorithm’s timing choice and an exact description of offline cost. The lower-bound part of that description then extends to many types without requiring a tree or a submodular spatial cost.

3.1 Why longer batches behave differently

Let requests arrive at rate λ\lambda and let one service cost cc, independently of the number of requests it serves. Immediate service has expected cost rate λ​c\lambda c. If we instead clear the queue every HH time units, a nonempty batch costs at most c+Hc+H. Its long-run cost rate is therefore at most

1+cH.1+\frac{c}{H}.

A longer period spreads the purchase over more time, while the maximum delay contributes at most one unit per unit time. Unlike additive delay, more arrivals do not create additional waiting charges inside the same batch. This suggests choosing between immediate service and large shared batches, with benchmark rate min⁡{λ​c,1}\min\{\lambda c,1\}. It remains to compare this choice with an optimum that sees the future.

3.2 Draw one interval per request

For every request arriving at aa, draw the interval [a,a+c][a,a+c]. Suppose a batch is served at time tt, and its first request arrived at a−a_{-}. All its request intervals lie inside [a−,t+c][a_{-},t+c]. That envelope has length c+t−a−c+t-a_{-}, exactly the cost of the batch. Taking the union of request intervals thus gives a lower bound on the cost of any schedule.

At one location this lower bound is exact. Group consecutive arrivals whose intervals overlap, and serve each group at its last arrival. The cost is precisely the length of that connected interval component. For example, with c=1c=1 and arrivals at 00, 0.40.4, and 22, the union is [0,1.4]∪[2,3][0,1.4]\cup[2,3]. Its length is 2.42.4, attained by serving the first two requests at 0.40.4 and the last at 22. Serving all three together would cost 33.

This representation converts offline optimization into a coverage calculation. Away from the beginning and end of the input horizon, a point is uncovered precisely when the preceding interval of length cc contains no arrival. Hence

limT→∞𝔼⁡[OPTT]T=1−e−λ​c.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]}{T}=1-e^{-\lambda c}.

The key is that these request intervals are fixed by arrivals and singleton costs. We do not try to apply a Poisson formula to intervals chosen by the offline schedule.

3.3 Which properties of a spatial service do we need?

For each type xx, let sxs_{x} be an attainable minimum spatial cost of serving one request alone. We require every batch serving xx to have spatial cost at least sxs_{x}. We also require one fixed action that serves any multiset of pending requests for spatial cost at most some finite MM, independent of multiplicities. These conditions concern stateless services; all spatial costs are paid anew at each event.

Now draw [ai,ai+sxi][a_{i},a_{i}+s_{x_{i}}] for request ii. If its batch has spatial cost CC, every interval in that batch lies in [a−,t+C][a_{-},t+C]. The same envelope argument proves

OPTT≥|⋃i∈IT[ai,ai+sxi]|.\operatorname{OPT}_{T}\geq\left|\bigcup_{i\in I_{T}}[a_{i},a_{i}+s_{x_{i}}]\right|.

Unlike the one-location case, equality is not needed or asserted. The singleton costs supply the lower bound; the universal action will supply an online upper bound.

Write L=∑xλx​sxL=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}s_{x}, the cost rate of immediate singleton service. Independence gives coverage probability 1−e−L1-e^{-L} away from the initial boundary. Thus the lower bound has long-run rate p=1−e−Lp=1-e^{-L}. It counts the union of time intervals, not their sum, so a batch’s single maximum-delay charge is never used repeatedly.

3.4 The algorithm and the constant

Let ρ=e/(e−1)\rho=e/(e-1). The algorithm makes one decision from the known instance before arrivals begin.

  • •

    If L≤1L\leq 1, serve each request immediately by a cheapest singleton action. The expected rate is LL, and L/(1−e−L)≤ρL/(1-e^{-L})\leq\rho for 0<L≤10<L\leq 1.

  • •

    If L>1L>1, use the universal action at regular times, skipping empty queues. A period HH gives cost rate at most 1+M/H1+M/H. Since ρ⁡(1−e−L)>1\rho(1-e^{-L})>1, a finite period can make this rate equal to the target ρ⁡(1−e−L)\rho(1-e^{-L}).

Explicitly, the second choice is

H=Mρ⁡(1−e−L)−1.H=\frac{M}{\rho(1-e^{-L})-1}.

At L=1L=1 the denominator would vanish, but immediate service already achieves the target there. Thus every instance uses either immediate service or a finite fixed period. Types with free singleton service are served immediately; if L=0L=0 all requests are free.

The result is a deterministic long-run ratio at most e/(e−1)e/(e-1). Every finite input finishes by the next scheduled clearing. The complete bound has an additive term depending on the instance, and an expensive universal action or a load just above one may yield a long period. Theorem 6.2 gives the finite-horizon bound; Section 6.6 explains why this policy need not have a uniform short-horizon ratio.

3.5 Why the factor is optimal

Return to one location with λ​c=1\lambda c=1. The offline rate is 1−e−11-e^{-1}. Any online policy must instead pay at rate at least one. The reason is a balance between an empty and a nonempty queue. While the queue is empty, a new arrival starts a batch that eventually needs a purchase. The expected rate of this purchase obligation is λ​c=1\lambda c=1. While the queue is nonempty, its oldest request accumulates waiting at unit rate. One of these two accounts is always active.

The formal proof first shows that clearing the whole queue can only help, then makes this accounting precise, including a batch unfinished at the horizon. It applies to randomized as well as deterministic causal policies. Therefore no universal factor below

11−e−1=ee−1\frac{1}{1-e^{-1}}=\frac{e}{e-1}

is possible. The complete sharpness argument follows the upper bound in Section 6.

3.6 Two tree applications

For multi-root aggregation, one request’s singleton cost is the cheapest root activation plus the path from that root to the client. One root and a subtree containing all possible clients provide a universal action. These two observations are enough: the offline optimum can still choose a different root for every batch.

For pair aggregation, a type’s singleton cost is the weight of its required endpoint path. A connected subtree containing all possible endpoints is a universal action. If a disconnected path union is allowed as one service, it may supply a cheaper universal action. We do not split one maximum-delay batch into multiple services while pretending that its delay charge stays unchanged.

Both models inherit e/(e−1)e/(e-1) from the same theorem, with no additional temporal loss. Section 7 verifies the actions and costs. The matching example is already a single positive edge. The general theorem needs neither a hierarchy of requirements nor submodularity; its two explicit spatial conditions are sufficient.

4 Facilities: connections change the comparison

A facility shares its opening among requests, but charges a separate connection distance to each occurrence. If kk requests lie at distance d>0d>0 from a facility of opening cost cc, serving them together costs c+k​dc+kd before delay. No fixed spatial bound independent of kk is available in this example. The universal-action theorem therefore cannot simply be applied to facility location.

We instead compute an assignment from a finite observed initial history and keep it fixed thereafter. The initial requests are served immediately, and all subsequent decisions are deterministic functions of the observed input and known instance data. The offline optimum remains free to choose a different facility for every request. The resulting deterministic long-run ratio is 33, with arbitrary nonnegative opening costs (Theorem 8.1). The expectation is over input arrivals alone.

4.1 Separate connections from opening and delay

Fix an assignment π\pi and let Λf\Lambda_{f} be the rate assigned to facility ff. Its expected connection cost rate is ∑xλx​d​(x,π⁡(x))\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}d(x,\pi(x)), regardless of service times. For opening plus maximum delay, immediate service has rate cf​Λfc_{f}\Lambda_{f}, whereas long collection periods approach rate one. The assignment should therefore make the following quantity small:

Ψ⁡(π)=∑xλx​d​(x,π⁡(x))+∑fmin⁡{cf​Λf,1}.\Psi(\pi)=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}d(x,\pi(x))+\sum_{f}\min\{c_{f}\Lambda_{f},1\}.

This is a target cost rate, not yet a complete service policy.

A useful reformulation chooses which facilities will support shared batches first. Each chosen facility contributes one unit to the target rate. A client can either connect to one of those facilities or use its cheapest individual service. This gives a static location problem that includes both service modes. The equivalence is proved in Lemma 8.2; it is not an assumption that all facility opening costs equal one.

4.2 Choose an assignment from observed arrival gaps

Let bxb_{x} be the distance from type xx to its nearest facility and let sx=minf⁡{cf+d⁡(x,f)}s_{x}=\min_{f}\{c_{f}+d(x,f)\} be its cheapest individual service cost. List the positive-rate types in a fixed order x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} and put Λ=∑xλx\Lambda=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}. Serve the first mm requests of the merged arrival stream immediately, recording their times A1,…,AmA_{1},\ldots,A_{m} and setting A0=0A_{0}=0. At time σ=Am\sigma=A_{m}, compute

Exj=Λλxj​(Aj−Aj−1),1≤j≤m.E_{x_{j}}=\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda_{x_{j}}}(A_{j}-A_{j-1}),\qquad 1\leq j\leq m.

The type index xjx_{j} is fixed beforehand and need not be the type of the jjth actual request. The merged gaps are independent exponentials of rate Λ\Lambda, so the scaled values ExE_{x} are independent exponentials of their respective rates λx\lambda_{x}. No random number is generated by the policy.

Set rx=bx+Exr_{x}=b_{x}+E_{x}, keep the candidate only when rx<sxr_{x}<s_{x}, and process the candidates in increasing order of rx+bxr_{x}+b_{x}.

A candidate represents the facility set A⁡(x,rx)={f:d⁡(x,f)<rx}A(x,r_{x})=\{f:d(x,f)<r_{x}\}. Accept it if this entire set is disjoint from all previously accepted facility sets. Each accepted candidate selects a nearest facility to its center. The test uses the full facility sets, so it can detect a conflict at a facility that neither candidate selects. Finally, each type connects to the nearest selected facility if this is cheaper than its individual service, and uses its cheapest individual service otherwise.

The construction uses only the first mm observed gaps. If the input contains fewer than mm requests, all of them have already been served immediately. Conditional on the initialization history, the stream after σ\sigma is a fresh Poisson input with the original rates (Lemma 8.3). Algorithm 2 gives the complete deterministic policy, and Theorem 8.1 states its complexity.

4.3 Compare the same packing with the offline optimum

To analyze the assignment, consider an auxiliary Poisson process of radii on (0,sx)(0,s_{x}) for each type, with intensity λx\lambda_{x}. Apply the same greedy rule, counting accepted empty facility sets as well. Let μ\mu be the expected number of accepted points and write B0=∑xλx​bxB_{0}=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}b_{x}. Empty sets do not affect the selected facilities. For any type, only its first nonempty candidate can affect the selection, so the output has exactly the marginal assignment law of the observed-gap construction above.

The expected number of selected facilities is μ−B0\mu-B_{0}. Poisson insertion bounds the expected connection and individual-service charges by B0+2​μB_{0}+2\mu. Adding the two contributions gives

𝔼⁡[Ψ⁡(π)]≤3​μ.\mathbb{E}[\Psi(\pi)]\leq 3\mu.

The insertion argument uses the priority rx+bxr_{x}+b_{x}: a rejected ball shares a facility with an earlier accepted ball, whose selected facility is close enough to bound its connection cost.

The same packing count also gives an offline lower certificate. Request ii is active for sxis_{x_{i}} time units after its arrival. At time τ\tau in this interval, give it residual radius sxi−(τ−ai)s_{x_{i}}-(\tau-a_{i}) and apply the same greedy rule. Within a batch served at facility ff, at most one accepted ball contains ff at any time. The opening and the batch’s maximum wait pay for the integrated contribution of these portions. Each request’s remaining portion has length at most its connection distance to ff. Consequently, the integrated accepted count lower-bounds every offline schedule, even if that schedule changes facilities between occurrences.

Stationarity identifies the expected interior time-slice count with μ\mu. Concatenating optimal schedules for consecutive equal-length blocks removes the initial boundary loss and gives

𝔼⁡[OPTT]≥T​μfor every ​T>0.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}]\geq T\mu\qquad\text{for every }T>0.

Together, these comparisons imply

T​𝔼​[Ψ⁡(π)]≤3​𝔼​[OPTT].T\mathbb{E}[\Psi(\pi)]\leq 3\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}].

Section 8 proves both comparisons in full. The assignment inequality averages over the observed initial gaps. It uses only their marginal law and does not require independence between the assignment and the full input.

4.4 Realize the target rate and finish the input

After initialization, facilities with cf​Λf≤1c_{f}\Lambda_{f}\leq 1 serve their assigned requests immediately. The others use predetermined service times measured from σ\sigma, clearing their entire queues and skipping empty batches. The calendar has successive gap lengths cf,2​cf,3​cf,…c_{f},2c_{f},3c_{f},\ldots. Over a long horizon, the number of openings is sublinear, while the sum of maximum-wait charges is bounded by the elapsed calendar time. This realizes the target unit rate for each such facility.

Initialization has expected cost at most m​L/ΛmL/\Lambda, where L=∑xλx​sxL=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}s_{x}. The remaining horizon h=(T−σ)+h=(T-\sigma)_{+} and the assignment can be correlated, but nonnegativity gives

𝔼⁡[h​Ψ​(π)]≤T​𝔼​[Ψ⁡(π)]≤3​𝔼​[OPTT].\mathbb{E}[h\Psi(\pi)]\leq T\mathbb{E}[\Psi(\pi)]\leq 3\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}_{T}].

This is the step that transfers the assignment comparison to the policy using observed arrivals. The proof never factors this expectation into a product of expectations.

Every request has a finite next service time. The final clearing contributes a correction of order OI​(T+1)O_{I}(\sqrt{T}+1), which is included before taking the long-run ratio. The exact factor 33 therefore does not give a fixed bound on all individual waits. Lemma 8.6 proves the complete accounting. If bounded waiting is preferred, fixed periods cf/εc_{f}/\varepsilon at the scheduled facilities give factor 3​(1+ε)3(1+\varepsilon) for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, with explicit constant initialization and completion terms (Corollary 8.7).

Guide to the technical development.

The shared-service argument needs an interval lower bound, a calendar upper bound, and the one-location sharpness proof. The facility result adds an observed-gap initialization, an assignment bound, a time-slice packing certificate, and an explicit calendar realization. The following sections give these arguments in full, beginning with their probability tools. The shared factor is optimal over its class; no matching optimality claim is made for the facility factor.

5 Probability tools for the proofs

The preceding sections described the algorithms and the comparisons behind their guarantees. We now give the complete technical arguments. This section collects the Poisson identities used to average the lower-bound constructions; subsequent sections prove the model-specific estimates. The insertion identity counts the contribution of a point whose acceptance depends on the other sampled points. In the facility proof it is applied to an auxiliary Poisson process of radii, sampled independently of the actual arrivals. It is an analysis tool, not information supplied about future requests. The facility proof also uses the independent exponential gaps of a merged stream to compute its assignment from an observed initial history.

We write z+=max⁡{z,0}z_{+}=\max\{z,0\}, use 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} for the indicator of an event, and let |J||J| denote the length of a measurable time set. Charging intervals are half-open. Nonnegative terms permit exchanges of sums, integrals, and expectations by Tonelli’s theorem.

5.1 Poisson identities used in the proofs

For a rate-λ\lambda process, the number N⁡(J)N(J) of arrivals in an interval JJ has distribution

Pr⁡(N⁡(J)=k)=e−λ​|J|​(λ​|J|)kk!,𝔼⁡[N⁡(J)]=Var⁡(N⁡(J))=λ​|J|.\Pr(N(J)=k)=e^{-\lambda|J|}\frac{(\lambda|J|)^{k}}{k!},\qquad\mathbb{E}[N(J)]=\operatorname{Var}(N(J))=\lambda|J|.

Counts in disjoint intervals are independent. Conditional on nn arrivals in a finite interval, their unordered times are nn independent uniform points in that interval. In particular, for a nonnegative deterministic function gg,

𝔼⁡[∑ai∈[0,T]g⁡(ai)]=λ​∫0Tg⁡(t)​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a_{i}\in[0,T]}g(a_{i})\right]=\lambda\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,dt. (2)

Conditioning on the count proves this identity: the conditional expectation is n​T−1​∫0Tg⁡(t)​𝑑tnT^{-1}\int_{0}^{T}g(t)\,dt, and 𝔼⁡[n]=λ​T\mathbb{E}[n]=\lambda T. We use it, for example, with g⁡(t)g(t) equal to the wait until the next deterministic clock tick. Nonnegative integrands also allow us to exchange sums, integrals, and expectations by Tonelli’s theorem.

For independent streams, superposition adds their rates. Conversely, independently assigning an arrival a mark jj with probability qjq_{j} produces independent Poisson streams of rates qj​λq_{j}\lambda. The generating function 𝔼⁡[∏jzjNj]=exp⁡(λ​|J|​∑jqj​(zj−1))\mathbb{E}[\prod_{j}z_{j}^{N_{j}}]=\exp(\lambda|J|\sum_{j}q_{j}(z_{j}-1)) factors into the generating functions of these independent counts. These statements apply to marks chosen independently for each occurrence; arbitrary routing based on the future need not preserve a Poisson law.

The void probability is Pr⁡(N⁡(J)=0)=e−λ​|J|\Pr(N(J)=0)=e^{-\lambda|J|}. It remains valid for a deterministic interval that depends on the instance parameters. We will not apply it to intervals selected by an offline schedule after observing arrivals. Instead, our lower bounds first establish an inequality for every realized schedule and then average a certificate whose counting regions are fixed independently of that schedule.

We also use the following extension of (2), in which the contribution of a distinguished arrival depends on the other arrivals. The same identity on intervals of radii will be used for the facility packing construction.

Lemma 5.1 (Poisson insertion).

Fix xx, and let ux​(a,J)u_{x}(a,J) be a nonnegative measurable quantity defined for a distinguished type-xx request at time aa and a finite multiset JJ of other requests. Then

𝔼[∑i∈IT:xi=xux(ai,IT∖{i})]=λx∫0T𝔼[ux(a,IT)]da.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i\in I_{T}:\,x_{i}=x}u_{x}(a_{i},I_{T}\setminus\{i\})\right]=\lambda_{x}\int_{0}^{T}\,\mathbb{E}[u_{x}(a,I_{T})]\,da. (3)

On the right, ITI_{T} is an independent Poisson input to which the distinguished request can be added inside the definition of uxu_{x}.

Proof.

Condition on the number Nx=nN_{x}=n of type-xx arrivals. Their times are independent uniforms in [0,T][0,T], and exchangeability makes the sum on the left equal in expectation to nn times the contribution of one distinguished uniform time, with n−1n-1 other type-xx times. The identity n​Pr⁡(Nx=n)=λx​T​Pr⁡(Nx=n−1)n\Pr(N_{x}=n)=\lambda_{x}T\Pr(N_{x}=n-1) changes the latter n−1n-1 points back into an unconditional type-xx Poisson process. All other types retain their independent laws. Integrating the distinguished uniform time proves (3). No conditioning on an arrival at one prescribed time is needed. ∎

Arrivals observed by a causal policy.

In the sharpness proof we count arrivals finding the system empty. The relevant identity is the predictable form of (2): for a bounded nonnegative process H⁡(t)H(t) determined just before time tt,

𝔼⁡[∑ai∈[0,T]H⁡(ai)]=λ​𝔼​[∫0TH⁡(t)​𝑑t].\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a_{i}\in[0,T]}H(a_{i})\right]=\lambda\,\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}H(t)\,dt\right].

For a simple predictable process, constant on deterministic intervals with coefficients determined at their left endpoints, this follows from independent increments. Approximation by such processes gives the identity for predictable integrands. In particular it applies to the left-limit indicator of an empty queue under a causal policy, including a policy with independent internal randomness. This does not assert the identity for a state chosen using future arrivals.

6 A sharp theorem for shared services

We develop the core result in three steps. First, one location reveals an exact description of offline cost and the two service regimes. Next, singleton costs extend the lower bound to general shared services, and a universal action supplies the upper bound. Finally, we show that the resulting constant cannot be improved even by randomization. The same development keeps track of completion costs, which matter when a busy instance uses a long service period.

6.1 One location: the cost of combining requests

Consider one request location with rate λ>0\lambda>0 and a service cost c>0c>0, independent of the number of pending requests. This is a one-edge aggregation problem, or a single facility colocated with its clients. There is no spatial choice, but the one-location instance already exhibits the interval certificate and the timing tradeoff used in the general theorem.

Now the delay of a nonempty batch is the waiting time of its oldest request. Immediate service costs c​λ​Tc\lambda T in expectation. A fixed-period policy with period hh has at most T/h+1T/h+1 openings, and each nonempty batch has delay at most hh. Hence its total cost is at most (T/h+1)​(c+h)(T/h+1)(c+h). By taking hh large, its long-run upper rate approaches 11, independently of cc and λ\lambda. This motivates the proxy

mc​(λ)=min⁡{c​λ,1}.m_{c}(\lambda)=\min\{c\lambda,1\}. (4)

The upper rate 1+c/h1+c/h approaches one as the period grows. To see the exact behavior, skip empty periods. A complete period has expected opening cost c⁡(1−e−λ​h)c(1-e^{-\lambda h}) and expected maximum waiting

∫0h(h−u)​λ​e−λ​u​𝑑u=h−1−e−λ​hλ.\int_{0}^{h}(h-u)\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\,du=h-\frac{1-e^{-\lambda h}}{\lambda}.

Thus its exact long-run cost rate is

R⁡(h)=1+(c−1λ)​1−e−λ​hh.R(h)=1+\left(c-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)\frac{1-e^{-\lambda h}}{h}.

In the busy regime λ​c>1\lambda c>1, every finite period has rate strictly above one; at λ​c=1\lambda c=1, every finite period has rate exactly one. For λ​c<1\lambda c<1, it is below one. In all three cases, completing a finite input may require a service after TT, whose cost must still be included in the finite-horizon bound.

Here is the intuitive reason for the difference. Under additive delay, each extra arrival contributes its own waiting time. Making the period longer therefore becomes increasingly expensive when the stream is busy. Under maximum delay, a hundred later arrivals may join the oldest one without increasing the delay charge of that batch. The policy may therefore use a much longer period. The resulting rate calculation is simple, but it says little yet about an offline schedule that chooses batch boundaries after seeing all arrivals.

The one-site offline optimum.

For maximum delay, the one-site offline optimum has a particularly useful samplewise description. If arrival times are a1<⋯<ama_{1}<\cdots<a_{m}, then

OPT⁡(IT)=|⋃i=1m[ai,ai+c]|.\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})=\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}[a_{i},a_{i}+c]\right|. (5)

Each arrival draws an interval of length cc to its right. The union records precisely how much of the time line can be covered by grouping nearby arrivals: a run of overlapping intervals is served as one batch, while a gap larger than cc starts a new batch. This picture explains the identity before any expectation is taken. To prove the lower inequality, a batch served at tt with earliest arrival a−a_{-} has all intervals of its requests inside [a−,t+c][a_{-},t+c]; the latter interval has length c+t−a−c+t-a_{-}, exactly the batch cost. Union measure is subadditive across batches. For the reverse inequality, sort the arrivals and place consecutive ones in the same batch whenever their gap is at most cc. Serve each batch at its last arrival time. Its cost is cc plus the span from its first to its last arrival, which equals the length of that connected component of the interval union. Summing gives (5).

For times at least cc from the endpoints of [0,T][0,T], the probability that a fixed point is covered by this union is 1−e−λ​c1-e^{-\lambda c}. The two boundary pieces have total length at most 2​c2c, so integrating the coverage indicator and taking expectations gives

limT→∞𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(IT)]T=1−e−λ​c.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]}{T}=1-e^{-\lambda c}. (6)

This explains why min⁡{c​λ,1}\min\{c\lambda,1\} is a constant-scale online proxy: for z=λ​cz=\lambda c, 1−e−z≥(1−e−1)​min⁡{z,1}1-e^{-z}\geq(1-e^{-1})\min\{z,1\}. The inequality follows from the monotonic decrease of (1−e−z)/z(1-e^{-z})/z on (0,1](0,1] and monotonic increase of 1−e−z1-e^{-z} on [1,∞)[1,\infty). We next extend the interval argument to shared services using singleton spatial costs. Facility location will require a further step, because different requests in one batch pay separate connection distances.

A concrete interval example.

Suppose c=1c=1 and arrivals occur at 00, 0.40.4, and 22. The union is [0,1.4]∪[2,3][0,1.4]\cup[2,3], of length 2.42.4. Serving the first two requests at 0.40.4 costs 1+0.41+0.4, and serving the last at 22 costs 11. Serving all three at 22 would instead cost 1+2=31+2=3. The gap between the second and third arrivals makes another opening cheaper than continuing the first batch. This example also separates the interval drawn for a request from its actual waiting interval: the former has prescribed length cc, regardless of when the request is served.

Which part generalizes?

With several types, a batch may contain requests with different singleton costs. There need not be a schedule whose cost equals the union measure. The lower inequality, however, still holds: each singleton cost is at most the spatial cost of its batch, so all request intervals fit in one paid envelope. For the upper bound we need a different ingredient, namely an action that can serve all possible types for a fixed spatial cost. We state these two requirements separately rather than assuming the one-location identity remains exact.

6.2 The shared-service model and its lower bound

We formulate the argument for the following class of services, then apply it to our two tree problems. Assume a stateless batch-service model with nonnegative spatial costs and the following properties. For each request type xx, the minimum singleton spatial cost sx≥0s_{x}\geq 0 is finite and attained. Every batch with spatial cost CC satisfies C≥sxC\geq s_{x} for each request location xx in the batch. Finally, a fixed action can serve any multiset of requests at all locations for spatial cost at most a finite constant MM. In particular, this cost does not grow with request multiplicity. We first prove the statement in this abstract form and then specify the two tree actions to which it applies. Discard zero-rate types first. If none remain, use the empty schedule: both costs are zero and no ratio is asserted. Below we assume at least one positive-rate type remains.

Notation.

Put

L=∑xλx​sx,s∗=maxx⁡sx,p=1−e−L,ρ∗=11−e−1.L=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}s_{x},\qquad s_{*}=\max_{x}s_{x},\qquad p=1-e^{-L},\qquad\rho_{*}=\frac{1}{1-e^{-1}}.

The number LL is the expected singleton spatial cost arriving per unit time. It is not itself a lower bound on offline cost, since several requests may share one service. The interval certificate below converts these singleton costs into a lower bound without charging any spatial purchase twice. Its construction is independent of how an offline schedule later chooses to group the requests.

Lemma 6.1 (Interval-union certificate).

For every finite input and every feasible schedule SS,

|⋃i[ai,ai+sxi]|≤cost⁡(S).\left|\bigcup_{i}[a_{i},a_{i}+s_{x_{i}}]\right|\leq\operatorname{cost}(S).

Consequently,

𝔼[OPT(IT)]≥∫0T[1−exp{−∑xλxmin(sx,t)}]dt≥p(T−s∗)+.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]\geq\int_{0}^{T}\left[1-\exp\left\{-\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\min(s_{x},t)\right\}\right]dt\geq p(T-s_{*})_{+}. (7)
Proof.

A service at time tt with spatial cost CC and earliest arrival a−a_{-} has every one of its request intervals inside [a−,t+C][a_{-},t+C]. That interval has length C+t−a−C+t-a_{-}, the service cost. Subadditivity of union measure proves the samplewise inequality, simultaneously for all schedules.

In more detail, each member ii arrived no earlier than a−a_{-} and is served at t≥ait\geq a_{i}. The assumption sxi≤Cs_{x_{i}}\leq C gives

ai+sxi≤t+C,a_{i}+s_{x_{i}}\leq t+C,

so its whole interval lies in that one envelope. We take a union inside each batch and then across batches. Overlapping envelopes only reduce the measure of the final union; the presence of several roots cannot create an additional charge.

At a time t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], absence of coverage means that every type xx has no arrival in [max⁡(0,t−sx),t][\max(0,t-s_{x}),t]. Independence and the Poisson void probability give the displayed integrand. For t≥s∗t\geq s_{*} it equals pp. The intervals intersected with [0,T][0,T] have length min⁡(sx,t)\min(s_{x},t), which explains the boundary term in the first integral rather than silently replacing it by a stationary rate at time zero. Integrating only over [s∗,T][s_{*},T] gives p​(T−s∗)+p(T-s_{*})_{+}. This argument never conditions on OPT’s service times. ∎

Figure 3 illustrates the only samplewise step: each request interval fits inside the envelope paid by the service that contains it. Intervals from different roots or disconnected portions of the tree are united only after this containment is proved. Their overlaps can only reduce the measure, so neither several roots nor a shared edge is charged repeatedly.

6.3 Deriving the online policy

The lower bound has rate p=1−e−Lp=1-e^{-L}. What rate can a simple policy attain? Immediate service costs exactly LL in expectation per unit time. The ratio L/(1−e−L)L/(1-e^{-L}) increases from 11 to ρ∗\rho_{*} as LL increases from 00 to 11. Thus no batching is needed in this range. If L>1L>1, immediate service can be expensive, but the target rate ρ∗​p\rho_{*}p is strictly greater than one.

A calendar with period HH pays at most MM spatially and HH in maximum delay per nonempty tick. Its asymptotic upper rate is therefore 1+M/H1+M/H. We choose the period by solving

1+M/H=ρ∗​p,givingH=Mρ∗​p−1.1+M/H=\rho_{*}p,\qquad\text{giving}\qquad H=\frac{M}{\rho_{*}p-1}.

The denominator is positive exactly in the busy regime L>1L>1. At L=1L=1 it would vanish, but immediate service already attains the desired factor there. This explains both the threshold and the period, including why an infinite period is never needed. Skipping an empty tick only improves the cost bound.

The policy depends on the instance before execution and on the current queue during execution. It does not inspect the horizon or predict a future arrival. An expensive universal action can make HH large, which is why we will also state its finite-horizon correction rather than interpreting the asymptotic ratio as a uniform short-horizon guarantee.

6.4 The guarantee, including completion costs

Theorem 6.2 (Sharp shared-connection guarantee).

For every fixed instance with L>0L>0, there is a horizon-unaware online algorithm with

RoE⁡(ALG)≤ρ∗=ee−1.\operatorname{RoE}(\operatorname{ALG})\leq\rho_{*}=\frac{e}{e-1}.

For each fixed instance with L>0L>0, the algorithm can use a finite, fixed maximum waiting time. The universal long-run factor ρ∗\rho_{*} is optimal over this model class, already for a single request location. When L=0L=0, every positive-rate type has free singleton service and both costs are identically zero; no ratio is defined.

Upper bound and explicit finite-horizon correction.

In every regime, requests with sx=0s_{x}=0 are served immediately at zero cost and excluded from the pending queue. If L=0L=0, all positive-rate requests have free singleton service. If 0<L≤10<L\leq 1, serve each request immediately at singleton cost. Thus 𝔼⁡[ALG⁡(IT)]=L​T\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T})]=LT. The function L/(1−e−L)L/(1-e^{-L}) is increasing for L>0L>0: its derivative has numerator 1−(1+L)​e−L>01-(1+L)e^{-L}>0. Hence

𝔼⁡[ALG⁡(IT)]≤ρ∗​𝔼​[OPT⁡(IT)]+L​s∗.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T})]\leq\rho_{*}\,\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]+Ls_{*}.

If L>1L>1, then M>0M>0 and δ=ρ∗​p−1>0\delta=\rho_{*}p-1>0. Choose the fixed period

H=Mρ∗​p−1.H=\frac{M}{\rho_{*}p-1}.

At H,2​H,3​H,…H,2H,3H,\ldots, use the universal action on all pending positive-cost requests, skipping empty batches. Every batch costs at most M+HM+H. On input ITI_{T}, all requests are served by ⌈T/H⌉​H\lceil T/H\rceil H, without an end signal. Therefore, pathwise,

ALG⁡(IT)≤(T/H+1)​(M+H)=ρ∗​p​T+M+H.\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T})\leq(T/H+1)(M+H)=\rho_{*}pT+M+H.

Combining this with (7) gives

𝔼⁡[ALG⁡(IT)]≤ρ∗​𝔼​[OPT⁡(IT)]+M+H+ρ∗​p​s∗.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T})]\leq\rho_{*}\,\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]+M+H+\rho_{*}ps_{*}. (8)

The correction is independent of TT but depends on the fixed instance. Dividing by the linearly growing optimum proves the long-run claim. No period tending to infinity during execution is needed for this theorem. ∎

6.5 Sharpness of the universal factor

The upper bound compares two explicit policies with interval coverage. To prove that the constant is inherent, we must compare every causal policy with the offline optimum. We return to one location with λ​c=1\lambda c=1, the transition between the two regimes. The offline rate is already known from (6). The remaining task is to show that every online algorithm pays at least one unit per unit time in expectation.

The reason is a balance between two states. While its queue is empty, arrivals occur at rate λ\lambda and start new busy periods. Each such period eventually requires a service costing cc. While its queue is nonempty, its oldest request accumulates maximum waiting at unit rate. Since λ​c=1\lambda c=1, either state contributes at the same expected rate. The proof below first justifies clearing the entire queue and then makes this accounting precise, including a busy period unfinished at TT.

Sharpness of Theorem 6.2.

Consider one location with spatial service cost c>0c>0 and rate λ\lambda, where λ​c=1\lambda c=1. For arrivals a1<⋯<ana_{1}<\cdots<a_{n}, the offline optimum is

0(n=0),c+∑i=2nmin⁡(c,ai−ai−1)(n≥1).0\quad(n=0),\qquad c+\sum_{i=2}^{n}\min(c,a_{i}-a_{i-1})\quad(n\geq 1).

Indeed, consecutive batches suffice: between consecutive requests one chooses independently either to span the gap or to pay another opening. Alternatively, this expression is precisely the measure of ⋃i[ai,ai+c]\bigcup_{i}[a_{i},a_{i}+c], so the interval certificate and this batching construction establish exact equality. The Poisson void calculation, with at most cc of initial and terminal boundary length, yields

limT→∞𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(IT)]T=1−e−1.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]}{T}=1-e^{-1}.

It suffices to consider algorithms that clear all pending requests at every opening. To justify this for the maximum-delay objective, retain any original causal algorithm’s opening times and move each request to the first opening at or after its arrival. An original batch may split among earlier openings, but its fragments’ waiting intervals are disjoint subintervals of its original waiting interval. Hence their summed maximum delays do not exceed the original delay. Merging fragments at an opening reduces this sum, and the number of openings does not grow.

The transformation is causal by simulating the original virtual state. Empty openings can be deleted.

For a full-clear algorithm, let Z⁡(t)Z(t) indicate a pending request, let A⁡(T)A(T) count arrivals finding the system empty, and let K⁡(T)K(T) count nonempty openings by TT. Then Z⁡(T)=A⁡(T)−K⁡(T)Z(T)=A(T)-K(T), starting empty.

Each period with Z⁡(t)=1Z(t)=1 runs from the first arrival after an opening to the next opening. Its length is exactly that opening’s maximum waiting charge. The integral through TT also counts the elapsed waiting of a final unfinished batch, whose eventual full delay can only be larger.

The independent-increment Poisson compensator identity uses the predictable empty-state indicator 1−Z⁡(t−)1-Z(t-) and gives

𝔼⁡[A⁡(T)]=λ​𝔼​[∫0T(1−Z⁡(t−))​𝑑t].\mathbb{E}[A(T)]=\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[\int_{0}^{T}(1-Z(t-))\,dt].

The left and right versions of ZZ differ only at jump times, which form a measure-zero set for the time integral below. Using λ​c=1\lambda c=1, the opening cost through TT plus holding accrued through TT equals, in expectation,

c​𝔼​[K⁡(T)]+𝔼⁡[∫0TZ⁡(t)​𝑑t]=T−c​𝔼​[Z⁡(T)].c\,\mathbb{E}[K(T)]+\mathbb{E}[\int_{0}^{T}Z(t)\,dt]=T-c\,\mathbb{E}[Z(T)].

If Z⁡(T)=1Z(T)=1, completion requires an additional opening costing cc; future waiting is nonnegative. Thus the full expected cost is at least TT for every causal algorithm. This also holds for randomized algorithms with independent randomness and even when TT is announced in advance. If expected cost is infinite the lower bound is immediate. Dividing by the offline rate proves the sharp factor ρ∗\rho_{*}. ∎

6.6 A limitation at finite horizons

Proposition 6.3 (No uniform finite-horizon ratio for this algorithm).

The algorithm of Theorem 6.2, including implementations that reduce the spatial service to the actual pending locations, has unbounded ratio on some fixed finite horizons as the instance varies.

Proof.

Take a path rooted at 00, with request locations 11 and M>1M>1, rates 22 and M−3M^{-3}, and no activation charge. Then s1=1,sM=Ms_{1}=1,s_{M}=M, L=2+M−2L=2+M^{-2}, and universal spatial cost is MM. The algorithm’s period is H=M/(ρ∗​(1−e−L)−1)H=M/(\rho_{*}(1-e^{-L})-1), with H/M→eH/M\to e. Take T=1T=1 and sufficiently large MM so that H>1H>1. The event that there is exactly one near request and no far request has probability

2​e−(2+M−3).2e^{-(2+M^{-3})}.

Conditional on this event its arrival is uniform in [0,1][0,1], and its cost is at least 1+H−a1+H-a, with conditional expectation H+1/2H+1/2. On the other hand, immediate singleton service gives 𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(I1)]≤2+M−2\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{1})]\leq 2+M^{-2}. Thus

𝔼⁡[ALG⁡(I1)]𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(I1)]≥2​e−(2+M−3)​(H+1/2)2+M−2⟶∞.\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}(I_{1})]}{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{1})]}\geq\frac{2e^{-(2+M^{-3})}(H+1/2)}{2+M^{-2}}\longrightarrow\infty.

This disproves a uniform finite-horizon claim for this algorithm, not the existence of some other algorithm with such a guarantee. ∎

The theorem is therefore a statement about each fixed instance as TT grows. It does not assert an instance-uniform horizon at which the boundary term becomes small. The spatial hypotheses also remain essential: the abstract theorem does not supply algorithms for computing cheapest singleton actions, and a persistent server or a per-occurrence connection sum requires further analysis.

7 Verification of the tree applications

We now allow the requests to specify spatial connections in a tree. In multi-root aggregation the service may select a root for each batch; in pair aggregation each request specifies two endpoints. The common idea is to identify what one request costs alone and what one fixed action costs when every possible type is present. Once these two actions are available, Section 6 already supplies the temporal algorithm and its full analysis.

Notation and service conventions.

Let 𝒯=(V,E)\mathcal{T}=(V,E) be a finite tree with nonnegative edge costs. In multi-root aggregation, requests occur at client vertices; a service chooses one root rr from a finite nonempty set RR and a connected subtree containing rr and every client in its batch. It pays the subtree cost and a root activation cr≥0c_{r}\geq 0. Each service purchases its network anew, and the offline optimum may change roots between services.

In pair aggregation, a type has endpoints ui,viu_{i},v_{i} and requires their unique path PiP_{i}. A connected service can buy the hull of the paths of its batch. We also allow the variant in which one service may purchase their union as a forest. The shared-service theorem applies to either convention, with the corresponding singleton and universal actions. A forest is not silently split into several maximum-delay services: such a split may increase the temporal charge.

If no positive-rate request type remains, use the empty schedule. In the constructions below, we assume that at least one type remains.

7.1 Multi-root aggregation

Idea.

For light demand, choose the cheapest root separately for each arrival. For heavy demand, select a single root and a subtree covering all possible clients, and share that action at calendar ticks. The offline optimum retains its freedom to change roots; the singleton interval certificate, rather than a restriction on that optimum, pays for the online policy.

Singleton and universal actions.

For multi-root aggregation, retain the original tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} and its terminal set RR. A singleton at xx can be served from its cheapest root, so

sx=minr∈R⁡{cr+d𝒯​(r,x)}.s_{x}=\min_{r\in R}\{c_{r}+d_{\mathcal{T}}(r,x)\}.

Every service containing xx pays at least sxs_{x}: its chosen subtree contains the entire root-to-xx path and pays that root’s activation. Let XX be the finite set of positive-rate client locations. Choose a root r0r_{0} minimizing

Mr=cr+w⁡(hull𝒯⁡({r}∪X)),M=minr∈R⁡Mr.M_{r}=c_{r}+w\bigl(\operatorname{hull}_{\mathcal{T}}(\{r\}\cup X)\bigr),\qquad M=\min_{r\in R}M_{r}.

At any nonempty tick, the subtree realizing MM can serve all queued clients, regardless of multiplicity. This gives every hypothesis of Theorem 6.2. It also explains why the heavy-case algorithm need not decide a different root for each batch: its universal root is paid for by the interval-union lower bound in expectation.

7.2 Pair aggregation

Idea.

A pair request must receive its entire endpoint path. The path cost is therefore a lower bound on any batch serving it, even when other paths overlap. A hull containing every possible endpoint is a universal connected service. If disconnected unions are legal as a single action, their smaller cost may be used instead. We do not split one maximum-delay batch into separate actions and assume that its delay remains unchanged.

Notation and actions.

For pair aggregation, type ii requires the unique tree path Pi=P𝒯​(ui,vi)P_{i}=P_{\mathcal{T}}(u_{i},v_{i}). Its singleton spatial cost is si=w⁡(Pi)s_{i}=w(P_{i}). Any legal service containing that type contains PiP_{i}, so its spatial cost is at least sis_{i}. A universal connected action is the hull of all positive-rate endpoints,

M=w(hull𝒯({ui,vi:λi>0})).M=w\bigl(\operatorname{hull}_{\mathcal{T}}(\{u_{i},v_{i}:\lambda_{i}>0\})\bigr).

It contains every required path. If the model permits a forest service, one may instead use the union ⋃iPi\bigcup_{i}P_{i}, with potentially smaller MM. Either action has cost independent of the number of queued occurrences. Thus the same theorem applies without assigning a common root to pair demands.

7.3 Algorithm and guarantee

Compute the corresponding singleton costs and universal action, and run Algorithm 1 without changing its threshold or calendar. For light demand it uses the singleton actions; otherwise it uses the chosen universal action on all queued requests. Every batch dominates each member’s singleton cost, and the universal cost does not depend on multiplicity. The shared-service theorem therefore gives the following result.

Corollary 7.1 (Both maximum-delay tree extensions).

For each fixed finite tree instance with L>0L>0, Algorithm 1 has long-run RoE at most e/(e−1)e/(e-1) in multi-root aggregation and pair aggregation with per-batch maximum waiting. Its finite-horizon correction is L​s∗Ls_{*} in the light regime and M+H+ρ∗​p​s∗M+H+\rho_{*}ps_{*} in the heavy regime.

8 Proof of the facility guarantee

We now consider a batch served by opening a facility and connecting each of its requests. The delay is still one maximum wait for the batch, but each occurrence pays its own connection distance. This changes the spatial part of the problem even when the set of possible client locations is finite.

Idea and illustration.

Suppose a client is at distance d>0d>0 from the only facility. Serving kk occurrences together costs c+k​dc+kd before delay. There is consequently no universal action of bounded cost independent of multiplicity. The shared-service theorem cannot simply be applied with the facility as that action. Yet under a fixed assignment, connection cost has a predictable rate, λ​d\lambda d, and only the opening-plus-delay part benefits from batching. This suggests first constructing a good assignment and then using the one-facility service rule on each assigned stream.

For the assignment, we scale observed arrival gaps from an initial sequence of immediately served requests. These values have independent exponential laws, and the future stream is independent of that observed history. We use the resulting radii to greedily select balls whose facility sets are disjoint. An auxiliary Poisson sample makes the connection between this construction and the offline lower bound explicit. At each time slice, apply the same packing rule to shrinking balls associated with active requests. Within any offline batch, the portions containing its facility are paid by its opening and maximum wait, while the remaining portions are paid by connections. Poisson insertion bounds the assignment cost by three times the expected packing size. Stationarity and offline subadditivity compare that size with unrestricted OPT. We then account for initialization and give shifted service calendars that include all completion costs. Every action of the policy is a deterministic function of the observed input.

8.1 The facility model

Notation.

Let (X∪F,d)(X\cup F,d) be a finite metric space, where XX contains possible request locations and F≠∅F\neq\varnothing contains possible facility locations. The sets may overlap. All distances are finite, and each facility ff has a finite opening cost cf≥0c_{f}\geq 0. Nothing requires opening costs to be uniform. Distinct requests at the same point remain distinct occurrences. We write (z)+=max⁡{z,0}\left(z\right)_{+}=\max\{z,0\}.

At time tt, an algorithm may choose f∈Ff\in F and a nonempty subset BB of pending requests whose arrival times aia_{i} satisfy ai≤ta_{i}\leq t. It pays cfc_{f} and connects each i∈Bi\in B to ff, paying d⁡(xi,f)d(x_{i},f) for that request. The facility closes after this event; opening it at another time costs again. Several service events at one time are allowed, but each has its own opening and delay charge. There is no capacity constraint or travel time.

cost⁡(B,f,t)=cf+∑i∈Bd⁡(xi,f)+maxi∈B⁡(t−ai).\operatorname{cost}(B,f,t)=c_{f}+\sum_{i\in B}d(x_{i},f)+\max_{i\in B}(t-a_{i}). (9)

The total cost is the sum over service events. The offline optimum may choose different facilities for different occurrences of the same type. The algorithm knows the metric, all opening costs, and all arrival rates. Each event pays its own maximum-wait charge, even when several events occur at the same time. The connection sum grows with request multiplicity; there need not be a universal action of bounded spatial cost.

8.2 A deterministic factor-three guarantee

We use the facility model of Section 8.1. The algorithm first serves a finite number of requests immediately. It then computes an assignment from their observed arrival gaps and uses deterministic service times for each assigned stream. An auxiliary Poisson packing bounds the assignment cost, and the same packing rule applied to time slices gives an offline lower certificate.

Discard zero-rate types and list the remaining types in a fixed order x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}. If m=0m=0, use the empty policy. For m>0m>0, write

Λ=∑xλx,sx=minf⁡{cf+d⁡(x,f)},bx=minf⁡d⁡(x,f),L=∑xλx​sx.\Lambda=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x},\qquad s_{x}=\min_{f}\{c_{f}+d(x,f)\},\qquad b_{x}=\min_{f}d(x,f),\qquad L=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}s_{x}.

For an assignment π:X→F\pi:X\to F, define

Λf=∑x:π⁡(x)=fλx,Ψ(π)=∑xλxd(x,π(x))+∑fmin{cfΛf,1},Φ=minπΨ(π).\Lambda_{f}=\sum_{x:\pi(x)=f}\lambda_{x},\qquad\Psi(\pi)=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}d(x,\pi(x))+\sum_{f}\min\{c_{f}\Lambda_{f},1\},\qquad\Phi=\min_{\pi}\Psi(\pi).

The opening-plus-delay term chooses between immediate service, of rate cf​Λfc_{f}\Lambda_{f}, and a calendar whose asymptotic rate is at most one. The following theorem realizes this proxy after a finite initialization phase.

Theorem 8.1.

For every finite metric facility instance with nonnegative opening costs and independent Poisson arrivals, Algorithm 2 is deterministic. When m>0m>0, its completed cost satisfies, for every T>0T>0,

𝔼⁡[ALG⁡(IT)]≤3​𝔼​[OPT⁡(IT)]+m​LΛ+2​∑f∈F(2​cf​T+cf).\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}(I_{T})]\leq 3\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]+\frac{mL}{\Lambda}+2\sum_{f\in F}\bigl(\sqrt{2c_{f}T}+c_{f}\bigr).

Consequently its long-run RoE is at most 33 on every instance with positive optimal asymptotic cost. The algorithm uses the first mm observed arrival gaps and O⁡(|X|​|F|+|X|​log⁡|X|)O(|X||F|+|X|\log|X|) arithmetic, comparison, and set operations to compute its assignment, with no auxiliary randomness.

The expectation is over the input arrivals alone. The assignment becomes fixed after initialization; it is not chosen before arrivals begin. The offline comparator remains unrestricted and may choose a different facility for each occurrence. The operation count uses the real-arithmetic model with exact observed timestamps.

8.3 The static proxy and the assignment algorithm

Put B0=∑xλx​bxB_{0}=\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}b_{x}. Fix a nearest facility n⁡(x)n(x) and a singleton minimizer g⁡(x)g(x), so that d⁡(x,n⁡(x))=bxd(x,n(x))=b_{x} and cg⁡(x)+d⁡(x,g⁡(x))=sxc_{g(x)}+d(x,g(x))=s_{x}. All ties are broken by fixed orders. For S⊆FS\subseteq F, let

J⁡(S)=|S|+∑xλx​min⁡{sx,d⁡(x,S)},J(S)=|S|+\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\min\{s_{x},d(x,S)\},

with d⁡(x,∅)=+∞d(x,\varnothing)=+\infty. The unit term for a selected facility represents the saturated opening-plus-delay rate; its physical opening cost remains cfc_{f}. The following identity relates facility selection to fixed assignments.

Lemma 8.2.

One has Φ=minS⊆F⁡J⁡(S)\Phi=\min_{S\subseteq F}J(S). For each SS, assigning every type to a nearest facility in SS when d⁡(x,S)<sxd(x,S)<s_{x}, and to g⁡(x)g(x) otherwise, gives Ψ⁡(π)≤J⁡(S)\Psi(\pi)\leq J(S).

Proof.

For a fixed assignment, put in SS the facilities whose opening proxy uses the saturated term 11. Their assigned clients can connect within SS at no greater distance. Every other client can use singleton fallback for cost at most its assigned opening-plus-connection charge. Thus J⁡(S)≤Ψ⁡(π)J(S)\leq\Psi(\pi).

Conversely, consider the assignment induced by SS in the statement. Charge at most one for each facility in SS and charge cg⁡(x)c_{g(x)} per fallback occurrence in expectation. For each physical facility the actual opening proxy is no larger than the sum of these charges, including when it receives both direct and fallback assignments. Adding connections gives Ψ⁡(π)≤J⁡(S)\Psi(\pi)\leq J(S), proving the identity. ∎

The assignment map GG takes a positive vector (ex)(e_{x}) as input. For each type, form rx=bx+exr_{x}=b_{x}+e_{x} and retain it only if rx<sxr_{x}<s_{x}. Process the retained candidates in increasing order of rx+bxr_{x}+b_{x}. A candidate represents the facility set

A⁡(x,r)={f∈F:d⁡(x,f)<r}.A(x,r)=\{f\in F:d(x,f)<r\}.

Accept it when this entire set is disjoint from all previously accepted facility sets, and select its nearest facility n⁡(x)n(x). Assign each type to its nearest selected facility when that distance is below sxs_{x}, and to g⁡(x)g(x) otherwise. Disjointness is tested on the entire sets A⁡(x,rx)A(x,r_{x}), not only on the selected nearest facilities.

The online policy supplies the vector using observed arrivals. Let AjA_{j} be the time of the jjth request in the merged arrival stream, with A0=0A_{0}=0. Serve the first mm requests immediately at their singleton minimizers. At time σ=Am\sigma=A_{m}, compute

Exj=Λλxj​(Aj−Aj−1),1≤j≤m,E_{x_{j}}=\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda_{x_{j}}}(A_{j}-A_{j-1}),\qquad 1\leq j\leq m,

and set π=G⁡(E)\pi=G(E). The index xjx_{j} is the jjth type in the fixed order, not necessarily the type of the jjth arriving request. This computation uses no internally generated random numbers. If fewer than mm requests ever arrive, they have all been served immediately.

8.4 The law of the observed gaps

For analysis, couple all finite inputs to an infinite Poisson stream. This defines σ\sigma and π=G⁡(E)\pi=G(E) even when ITI_{T} has fewer than mm requests. The actual algorithm does not access this continuation. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the history of the first mm merged arrivals, including their times and types. The next lemma identifies both the marginal assignment law and the conditional law of the remaining input.

Lemma 8.3.

The variables ExE_{x} are independent and have distributions Exp⁡(λx)\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_{x}). Conditional on ℋ\mathcal{H}, the request streams strictly after σ\sigma, translated by −σ-\sigma, are independent Poisson streams of rates (λx)(\lambda_{x}), with a law independent of ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Proof.

Write Zj=Aj−Aj−1Z_{j}=A_{j}-A_{j-1} and let MjM_{j} be the type of the jjth merged request. For independent exponential clocks, the next gap ZZ and its winning type MM have joint density

Pr⁡(Z∈d​z,M=x)=λx​e−Λ​z​d​z=Λ​e−Λ​z​d​z⋅λxΛ.\Pr(Z\in dz,M=x)=\lambda_{x}e^{-\Lambda z}\,dz=\Lambda e^{-\Lambda z}\,dz\cdot\frac{\lambda_{x}}{\Lambda}.

Memorylessness restarts the independent clocks after each arrival. Thus the ZjZ_{j} are independent Exp⁡(Λ)\operatorname{Exp}(\Lambda) variables, the MjM_{j} are independent marks with probabilities λx/Λ\lambda_{x}/\Lambda, and the two sequences are independent. For u≥0u\geq 0,

Pr⁡(Exj>u)=Pr⁡(Zj>λxjΛ​u)=e−λxj​u.\Pr(E_{x_{j}}>u)=\Pr\left(Z_{j}>\frac{\lambda_{x_{j}}}{\Lambda}u\right)=e^{-\lambda_{x_{j}}u}.

The gaps and marks after index mm are independent of the first mm pairs and have their original laws. This proves the conditional future statement, including independence across types by the same exponential-clock description. ∎

8.5 An auxiliary Poisson packing

For the analysis, independently sample a Poisson process of radii with intensity λx​d​r\lambda_{x}\,dr on (0,sx)(0,s_{x}) for each positive-rate type xx. This finite auxiliary sample is independent of the actual arrival processes. Process all its points (x,r)(x,r) in increasing order of r+bxr+b_{x}, accepting a point precisely when A⁡(x,r)A(x,r) is disjoint from all earlier accepted facility sets. Empty sets are always accepted and select no facility. Every nonempty accepted set selects n⁡(x)n(x), which belongs to that set. Let SS be the selected facility set, KK the number of accepted points including empty sets, and μ=𝔼⁡[K]\mu=\mathbb{E}[K].

This conceptual construction has the same marginal assignment law as G⁡(E)G(E) in Algorithm 2, with EE defined on the infinite Poisson continuation. Indeed, the nonempty sets of any one type are nested as the radius increases. If its first nonempty point is accepted, it blocks every later point of that type. If that first point is rejected, its earlier accepted blocker also intersects every larger set of that type. Thus all later points are rejected and cannot affect the greedy output. Empty points block nothing and may also be omitted. The first point above bxb_{x} is distributed as bx+Exp⁡(λx)b_{x}+\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_{x}) and is present in the auxiliary interval exactly when it is smaller than sxs_{x}. Lemma 8.3 identifies this law with the vector computed from observed arrival gaps, proving the claimed equivalence. Computing the minima, testing set intersections by scanning FF, sorting at most |X||X| candidates, and forming the assignment takes O⁡(|X|​|F|+|X|​log⁡|X|)O(|X||F|+|X|\log|X|) operations.

The nonempty accepted sets are pairwise disjoint and contain their selected facilities, so those facilities are distinct. All sampled points with r≤bxr\leq b_{x} have empty sets and are accepted. Their expected number is B0B_{0}. Consequently

𝔼​|S|=μ−B0,μ≤B0+min⁡{|X|,|F|}.\mathbb{E}|S|=\mu-B_{0},\qquad\mu\leq B_{0}+\min\{|X|,|F|\}.

The next lemma bounds connections through insertion into this auxiliary sample.

Lemma 8.4.

The assignment π=G⁡(E)\pi=G(E) satisfies 𝔼⁡[Ψ⁡(π)]≤3​μ\mathbb{E}[\Psi(\pi)]\leq 3\mu.

Proof.

Let px​(r)p_{x}(r) be the probability that a distinguished point (x,r)(x,r) inserted into an independent auxiliary sample is accepted. If it is rejected, an earlier accepted point (y,u)(y,u) shares a facility hh with it and has u+by≤r+bxu+b_{y}\leq r+b_{x}. Insertion leaves every earlier greedy decision unchanged. The nearest facility n⁡(y)n(y) chosen for the blocker therefore belongs to the original sample’s set SS. The triangle inequality gives

d⁡(x,n⁡(y))≤d⁡(x,h)+d⁡(h,y)+by<r+u+by≤2​r+bx.d(x,n(y))\leq d(x,h)+d(h,y)+b_{y}<r+u+b_{y}\leq 2r+b_{x}.

Hence

Pr{d(x,S)>2r+bx}≤px(r).\Pr\{d(x,S)>2r+b_{x}\}\leq p_{x}(r).

For an empty inserted set the inequality also holds, since it is always accepted.

Since bx≤min⁡{sx,d⁡(x,S)}b_{x}\leq\min\{s_{x},d(x,S)\}, integration of the survival function gives

𝔼​∑xλx​min⁡{sx,d⁡(x,S)}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\min\{s_{x},d(x,S)\} =B0+∑xλx∫bxsxPr{d(x,S)>v}dv\displaystyle=B_{0}+\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\int_{b_{x}}^{s_{x}}\Pr\{d(x,S)>v\}\,dv
≤B0+2​∑xλx​∫0(sx−bx)/2px​(r)​𝑑r\displaystyle\leq B_{0}+2\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\int_{0}^{(s_{x}-b_{x})/2}p_{x}(r)\,dr
≤B0+2​∑xλx​∫0sxpx​(r)​dr=B0+2​μ.\displaystyle\leq B_{0}+2\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\int_{0}^{s_{x}}p_{x}(r)\,dr=B_{0}+2\mu.

The last equality is the Poisson insertion identity from Lemma 5.1, applied to radii instead of arrival times. Terms with sx=0s_{x}=0 vanish. For sx>0s_{x}>0, conditioning on the Poisson count NxN_{x} in (0,sx)(0,s_{x}) gives independent uniform radii, and the identity j​Pr⁡(Nx=j)=λx​sx​Pr⁡(Nx=j−1)j\Pr(N_{x}=j)=\lambda_{x}s_{x}\Pr(N_{x}=j-1) proves the same insertion formula on that interval. Finally, 𝔼​|S|=μ−B0\mathbb{E}|S|=\mu-B_{0} and Lemma 8.2 yield

𝔼⁡[Ψ⁡(π)]≤𝔼⁡[J⁡(S)]≤(μ−B0)+(B0+2​μ)=3​μ.\mathbb{E}[\Psi(\pi)]\leq\mathbb{E}[J(S)]\leq(\mu-B_{0})+(B_{0}+2\mu)=3\mu.

∎

8.6 The offline packing certificate

We now apply the same greedy rule to a time slice of the actual requests. The resulting certificate is valid for every realized schedule, independently of its facility choices.

Lemma 8.5.

For every T>0T>0, 𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(IT)]≥T​μ\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]\geq T\mu.

Proof.

For a finite realization ITI_{T} and time τ\tau, request ii is active when ai≤τ<ai+sxia_{i}\leq\tau<a_{i}+s_{x_{i}} and then has residual radius

ri​(τ)=sxi−(τ−ai).r_{i}(\tau)=s_{x_{i}}-(\tau-a_{i}).

Apply the auxiliary greedy rule to these active balls and let KT​(τ)K_{T}(\tau) count the accepted points, including empty sets. At every time, at most one accepted set contains any given facility. The integral of this count is a lower bound for every schedule 𝒮\mathcal{S}:

∫ℝKT​(τ)​𝑑τ≤cost⁡(𝒮).\int_{\mathbb{R}}K_{T}(\tau)\,d\tau\leq\operatorname{cost}(\mathcal{S}).

To prove this, fix a batch served at ff at time tt, and let a−a_{-} be its earliest arrival. Split the active interval of request ii into a prefix of length (sxi−d⁡(xi,f))+(s_{x_{i}}-d(x_{i},f))_{+} and the remaining tail, whose length is at most d⁡(xi,f)d(x_{i},f). During the prefix its ball contains ff, apart from endpoints of measure zero. The accepted prefix indicators of this batch sum to at most one at every time. Every such prefix lies in [a−,t+cf][a_{-},t+c_{f}], because sx≤cf+d⁡(x,f)s_{x}\leq c_{f}+d(x,f). Their integrated contribution is at most cf+t−a−c_{f}+t-a_{-}, and the tails contribute at most the sum of connection distances. Summing over batches proves the inequality, including batches completed after TT. Figure 4 illustrates the facility-set and time-slice constraints.

Let s∗=maxx⁡sxs_{*}=\max_{x}s_{x} over positive-rate types, with s∗=0s_{*}=0 if none remain. For τ∈[s∗,T]\tau\in[s_{*},T], each relevant arrival interval lies inside [0,T][0,T]. Mapping a type-xx arrival to its residual radius gives a Poisson process of intensity λx​d​r\lambda_{x}\,dr on (0,sx)(0,s_{x}), independently across types. Thus 𝔼​KT​(τ)=μ\mathbb{E}K_{T}(\tau)=\mu throughout this interior interval, and Tonelli’s theorem gives

𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(IT)]≥(T−s∗)+​μ.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]\geq(T-s_{*})_{+}\mu.

No independence between different time slices is required. The certificate is measurable: for finite ITI_{T}, its active sets and facility incidences change only finitely many times, and the relative priority of two simultaneously active points is constant.

Subadditivity removes the initial boundary term. Put V⁡(T)=𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(IT)]V(T)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})], which is finite since immediate singleton service has expected cost T​∑xλx​sxT\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}s_{x}. Each offline batch can be served at its latest arrival without increasing cost, so an optimal schedule for a block can finish within that block. Concatenating optimal schedules for ℓ\ell consecutive blocks of length TT gives V⁡(ℓ​T)≤ℓ​V​(T)V(\ell T)\leq\ell V(T). The blocks have identical Poisson laws, and deterministic endpoints contain no arrival almost surely. Applying the interior lower bound at horizon ℓ​T\ell T therefore yields

V⁡(T)≥(ℓ​T−s∗)+ℓ​μ.V(T)\geq\frac{(\ell T-s_{*})_{+}}{\ell}\mu.

Letting ℓ→∞\ell\to\infty proves V⁡(T)≥T​μV(T)\geq T\mu for every fixed T>0T>0. ∎

Together, Lemmas 8.4 and 8.5 give

Φ≤𝔼⁡[Ψ⁡(π)]≤3​μ≤3​𝔼⁡[OPT⁡(IT)]T.\Phi\leq\mathbb{E}[\Psi(\pi)]\leq 3\mu\leq 3\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(I_{T})]}{T}.

This comparison uses only the marginal law of π\pi. It asserts neither a bound for every realized assignment nor independence of π\pi from the full input. The next step conditions on the initialization history to use the independent future supplied by Lemma 8.3.

8.7 Service calendars, initialization, and completion

Let Cpost​(IT)C_{\mathrm{post}}(I_{T}) denote the cost after initialization, including completion after TT, and set h=(T−σ)+h=(T-\sigma)_{+}. Conditional on ℋ\mathcal{H}, the values of hh and π\pi are fixed. When σ>T\sigma>T, this cost is zero. Otherwise the future stream at ff is Poisson of rate Λf\Lambda_{f}. Immediate service realizes the proxy when cf​Λf≤1c_{f}\Lambda_{f}\leq 1. For the remaining facilities, the increasing service times make the average opening rate vanish while the total maximum-delay rate is at most one. The following estimate accounts for the final clearing.

Lemma 8.6.

For every T>0T>0, Algorithm 2 satisfies

𝔼[Cpost(IT)∣ℋ]≤hΨ(π)+2∑f:cf​Λf>1(2​cf​h+cf).\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{post}}(I_{T})\mid\mathcal{H}]\leq h\Psi(\pi)+2\sum_{f:c_{f}\Lambda_{f}>1}\bigl(\sqrt{2c_{f}h}+c_{f}\bigr).

Every finite input is cleared without an end-of-input signal.

Proof.

If h=0h=0, the cost is zero and the bound holds. For h>0h>0, condition on ℋ\mathcal{H} and measure time from σ\sigma. The expected connection cost is h​∑xλx​d​(x,π⁡(x))h\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}d(x,\pi(x)). An instant facility has opening-plus-delay rate cf​Λfc_{f}\Lambda_{f}. For a scheduled facility, cf>0c_{f}>0. Let JfJ_{f} be the first index with tf,Jf=cf​Jf​(Jf+1)/2≥ht_{f,J_{f}}=c_{f}J_{f}(J_{f}+1)/2\geq h, and put tf,0=0t_{f,0}=0. There are at most JfJ_{f} nonempty openings through completion.
